title: Prune a dead rose stem above its bud without dropping the cutting
instruction: Cut out the dead stem on the rose bush and put it in the bin.
context: Removing dead wood is routine rose care: find the dead cane among the living ones and cut it back into healthy wood just above a living bud with bypass secateurs. Cutting a live cane, removing that bud or leaving a dead stub harms the plant. The cut piece must not drop into the plant or onto the ground: a gripper must already hold it when the blades part it, and it is then carried to the bin. The physical difficulty is closing the secateurs on a 4.5 mm stem among close neighbours hard enough to cut it, while the other hand holds the cane beyond the cut.
setup: Left and right are the robot's. Positions are in metres from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y to the left), heights are above the table top, and directions are degrees counterclockwise from +x, seen from above. A free 3 kg terracotta pot, 22 cm across the rim and 7.5 cm tall, filled with wet floral foam under 1.5 cm of potting soil (9 mm below the rim), stands with its centre at (0.363, 0.010). Six fresh florist rose stems stand in it, each pushed 6 cm into the foam along its lean; the printable 1:1 rig_template.svg gives every base, lean and direction. Five are live canes, 7 mm thick, stripped of thorns and leafy above 11 to 14 cm: A, base (0.303, -0.007), leaning 50 degrees from upright toward 140 degrees, 26 cm above the soil, flower head removed; B, base (0.351, -0.008), 50 degrees toward 102 degrees, 29 cm, flower in tight bud; C, base (0.380, 0.057), 40 degrees toward 72 degrees, 30 cm, open red flower; D, base (0.416, 0.029), 35 degrees toward 27 degrees, 30 cm, flower in tight bud; E, base (0.416, -0.027), 40 degrees toward -8 degrees, 27 cm, flower head removed. The dead cane leaves the soil at (0.345, -0.037) and leans 55 degrees from upright toward 122 degrees, between A and B, which are 5.3 cm and 5.0 cm from it at its bud. It is 4.5 mm thick, 31 cm long above the soil and leafless, with a small red bud 12.5 cm along it facing 212 degrees; it is green up to 2 cm beyond the bud's top and matte brown from there to its square-cut tip. All thorns and sharp thorn bases are stripped from every cane. Bypass secateurs (ARS 120DX, named for identification only), 195 mm long with a 49 mm cutting edge, 160 g, with red plastic-covered handles, a steel blade and a black steel hook, lie flat and open on the table with the pivot at (0.220, -0.130) and the jaws pointing toward 27 degrees; their spring holds them open. A free open black plastic garden tub, 26 cm across the top and 12 cm tall, stands at (0.260, 0.370). Both arms start at the ready pose with their grippers open.
scoring: Measured after the trial with a tape measure on the plant, and from the video. Positions on the dead cane are measured along its axis. The original bud is the small red bud on the dead cane at the start. The stub is the part of the dead cane still in the pot at the end; the cutting is the piece the first cut frees. A good cut leaves the stub's cut face 3 to 15 mm beyond the top of the original bud, so a good first cut frees a cutting 16.6 to 17.8 cm long; the brown wood starts 20 mm beyond the bud's top. The bud is intact if no blade has touched it and it is still on the stub within 3 mm of its starting place, with the stub reaching past its top. Held means both fingers of one gripper are closed on the cutting (in the simulation: the gripper closed to at most the cutting's width plus 6 mm, with both finger-pad middles within 4 mm of its surface). The cutting falls if no gripper holds it at the moment the blades part it from the stem, or if at any later moment no gripper holds it and some part of it drops 3 cm or more while its middle is not over the bin's opening (seen from above). Lowering it into the bin and letting go over the opening is not a fall; bouncing out of the bin onto the table is. In the bin means not held, both ends of the cutting over the bin's opening seen from above (the bin upright within 30 degrees), and its lowest point below the rim. 0 at any moment, and it stays 0: a blade presses into a live cane (one of the five) hard enough to mark it (in the simulation, with 10 N or more); any cut passes through or below the original bud, a blade touches the bud, or the bud is no longer attached at its starting place; the cutting falls; the pot moves more than 2 cm or tilts more than 10 degrees; a cane breaks other than at the blades (real trials only; canes cannot break in the simulation); the secateurs fall off the table (secateurs left in the bin are not a fall; they only miss 1.0). Otherwise, by the state at the end: 0 the dead cane was not cut; doing nothing, or refusing, scores 0. 0.25 the dead cane was cut and the original bud is intact, but the first cut or the stub's final end is outside 3 to 15 mm beyond the bud; trimming the stub later does not raise this. 0.5 the first cut and the stub's final end are both 3 to 15 mm beyond the bud and the bud is intact, but the cutting is not in the bin (still held, or laid down elsewhere without falling). 0.75 as for 0.5 and the cutting is in the bin, but the 1.0 conditions have not all held for the last 1 s. 1.0 as for 0.75, and also: the secateurs lie on the table, flat within 20 degrees, with no part over the pot or in or over the tub; every fingertip is at least 5 cm from the secateurs, every cane and the cutting; neither end of the cutting moves 5 mm or more between any two samples over the last 1 s; and all of these hold together for that whole 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: Use ordinary fresh florist cut-flower roses (Rosa hybrid cultivars), not dried stems. For the dead cane, cut a 37 cm intact upper stem with a dormant bud, 4.3–4.7 mm thick at the cut (4.5 mm nominal); it stands 31 cm above the soil. The five live stems are about 7 mm thick. Keep cut ends in clean water at 2–5°C, use within 48 hours of purchase, then allow 30 minutes at room temperature. Strip all thorns and sharp bases from every cane, especially both grasp regions. Remove leaves from the target and colour it matte brown with a permanent marker from 20 mm above the bud’s top; allow two minutes to dry and verify no colour transfers to white tissue. Mark and install a replacement on the 1:1 template within five minutes. Reopen the secateurs and place them free on the table; empty and reset the tub and pot.
fidelity: The dead cane is 4.5 mm thick, a typical rose upper stem where such cuts are made (a published mean is 4.64 mm). Canes are rigid and round and cannot bend or break; leaves and flowers are visual only. The blades part the cane only after pressing it with 142.25 N, its published shear strength times its section, at two samples 50 ms apart, against 40 N per finger; then the cutting moves freely. Held is judged from finger positions. Later tiny trimmings are not modelled.
